analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to give workers pay disclosures and paystubs, and sharply raises penalties for wage theft.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate labor committee on the day it was introduced and never received a hearing, markup, or vote; it expired when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would amend federal wage law to combat wage theft — employers not paying workers the wages they are owed. It would require employers to tell workers their pay rate and classification when hired, provide itemized paystubs, pay all wages owed within 14 days of a firing, and let workers see their own pay records. It would also raise penalties for violators, triple the window for workers to sue, ban forced arbitration of wage claims, and fund community groups that help workers recover unpaid wages. It was introduced by Senator Patty Murray with 28 cosponsors, but the Senate committee it went to never acted on it.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers whose employers short them on pay — unpaid minimum wage, unpaid overtime, off-the-clock work, stolen tips, or late final paychecks. Low-wage workers, women, immigrants, and Black and Latino workers are hit hardest by wage theft, according to the findings Congress recorded in the bill itself. Law-abiding employers also gain, because firms that steal wages no longer undercut them.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Low-wage workers whose pay is shorted

how_it_helps.text: Employers must give new hires a written disclosure of their pay rate and whether they are classified as eligible for overtime, provide itemized paystubs showing hours, rates, and deductions, pay all final wages within 14 days of termination, and let employees inspect their own wage records going back five years [S2][S3].
Employers must pay the rate specified in an employment contract or union agreement even when it exceeds the minimum wage, and all unpaid wages become recoverable through civil enforcement [S2].

Civil fines rise to as much as $22,030 per employee per initial violation and $110,150 per employee for repeated or willful violations, employers who willfully falsify records and steal wages must be referred to the Department of Justice for criminal prosecution, and workers recover interest plus double or triple damages [S3].

The window to sue doubles from two years to four (five for willful violations), and workers can no longer be forced to sign away their right to go to court over wages as a condition of employment [S3].

The Department of Labor would distribute $50 million a year in grants to nonprofits, labor organizations, legal aid groups, and universities to educate workers about their rights and help them recover unpaid wages [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: Employers who currently underpay workers or skip required paperwork — concentrated in low-wage industries like restaurants, retail, janitorial services, agriculture, and staffing — would face new disclosure and paystub requirements, much larger fines and damage awards, a longer exposure to lawsuits, and possible criminal referral for willful violators. Compliant employers face compliance costs but gain a level playing field.

drawbacks.text: Small businesses would bear real compliance costs: written hire disclosures in the worker's primary language, detailed itemized paystubs, and fines of up to $100 per employee for repeated paperwork violations [S3].

The bill would override the Federal Arbitration Act to bar employers from forcing workers into arbitration over wage claims, a change critics of mandatory arbitration opponents describe as pushing disputes into costly class litigation; the bill itself also raises litigation exposure by doubling the statute of limitations and authorizing double and triple damages [S3].
Maximum civil fines of $110,150 per employee for willful violations are substantial enough that even employers who consider them excessive in individual cases would face severe financial risk [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers, the gains are direct: an estimated $15 billion a year in stolen wages is currently recovered only partially, and the bill's findings note that in some industries fewer than half of employers comply with federal wage law. The costs fall mainly on employers who are not complying now, plus compliance paperwork for everyone. The strongest honest objection is the litigation burden on small businesses, but the bill pairs its penalties with grants to help employers learn their obligations and with outreach aimed at the worst-violating industries rather than blanket enforcement.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee the day it was introduced and the committee never took it up; when the 117th Congress ended in January 2023, the bill died.

narrative.text: Senator Patty Murray introduced the bill on May 10, 2022, with 28 cosponsors — 27 Senate Democrats and 1 Senate Independent [S1][S4][S5].
It was read twice and referred the same day to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S5].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action at any point afterward [S5].
The Congress ended on January 3, 2023, and the bill expired without ever receiving a vote in either chamber [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers who underpay workers are better off, because none of the new paystub requirements, higher fines, longer lawsuit windows, or criminal referrals ever took effect, and the mandatory arbitration of wage claims remains in place.

for.name: Patty Murray
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and recruited 28 cosponsors

against.name: 50 of 50 Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: None of the 50 Senate Republicans cosponsored the bill, and the bill received no committee or floor action during the Congress

sides.party_line_note: All 28 cosponsors were Democrats or Independents; none of the 50 Senate Republicans signed on, and the bill never advanced beyond its referral to committee [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Low-wage service employers (restaurants, retail, janitorial, agriculture, staffing)
industries.note: These industries have the lowest federal wage-law compliance, and the bill's findings cite compliance below 50 percent in some sectors. The bill would cost violators unpaid wages plus interest, double or triple damages, fines up to $110,150 per employee, and possible criminal referral.

industries.industry: Employers and arbitration providers relying on mandatory arbitration clauses
industries.note: The bill would override the Federal Arbitration Act so that a worker's right to sue over wages in court, including as a class, could not be waived in a pre-dispute arbitration agreement. Employers could no longer route wage disputes into a private forum workers cannot appeal.
The bill's own findings state that wage theft puts compliant employers at a competitive disadvantage with noncompliant ones; higher penalties for violators would narrow that gap.

industries.industry: Nonprofit legal aid, labor organizations, and worker advocacy groups
industries.note: A new $50 million-a-year grant program would fund these groups to educate workers, assist with claims, and help recover unpaid wages alongside Labor Department enforcement.
